scenario.name: BPFDoor Passive Linux Rootkit & Classic BPF Magic Packet Filter (Red Menshen)
scenario.overview: Imagine a silent spy who moves into a temporary hallway locker inside a busy central post office, burns the paper lease behind them, and clips on a maintenance janitor badge. Instead of renting an office doorway that shows up on the building floor plan, the spy snaps a tiny acoustic sieve straight onto the main mail chute and sleeps invisibly for years until a single envelope carrying a secret wax seal drops past the chute, waking the spy to open a private back staircase. In this scenario (T1036.004, BPFDoor Passive Linux Rootkit & Classic BPF Magic Packet Filter (Red Menshen)), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: in-Memory /dev/shm/kdmtmpflush Execution, then attaching Kernel Berkeley Packet Filter, then magic Packet Activation, iptables Port. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering In-Memory /dev/shm/kdmtmpflush Execution, then Attaching Kernel Berkeley Packet Filter, then Magic Packet Activation, iptables Port, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: In-Memory /dev/shm/kdmtmpflush Execution, Unlinking & Process Masquerading
stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion (T1036.004 - Masquerade Task or Service / T1070.004)
stages.description: Upon entering the post office with master keys, the spy steps into a temporary memory-only hallway locker, backdates the locker stamp by more than a decade, shreds the locker key tag so nothing appears on the shelf, and pins on a routine building-service nametag. When launched as root, BPFDoor copied its ELF binary to /dev/shm/kdmtmpflush (the RAM-backed tmpfs shared memory filesystem), timestomped its modification date to 2008-10-30, re-executed itself with --init, immediately deleted /dev/shm/kdmtmpflush from the filesystem (leaving the process running purely in RAM while /proc/<pid>/exe pointed to /dev/shm/kdmtmpflush (deleted)), and called prctl(PR_SET_NAME) plus argv[0] overwriting to masquerade as hald-addon-acpi: listening on acpi kernel interface or /usr/libexec/postfix/master. Standard administrator checks like ps aux displayed a convincing Linux system daemon name, while disk-based antivirus scans found nothing because the executable file had already been unlinked. In the documented EventID 1 exchange from Red Menshen Operator (Magic Packet) to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ALERT 1 (confirming that the kdmtmpflush request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Attaching Kernel Berkeley Packet Filter via setsockopt(SO_ATTACH_FILTER)). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ kdmtmpflush / ⇠#1 ALERT 1) from Node ① (#1 Red Menshen Operator (Magic Packet)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Masqueraded Shell (/dev/shm/kdmtmpflush)).

stages.title: Stage 2: Attaching Kernel Berkeley Packet Filter via setsockopt(SO_ATTACH_FILTER)
stages.subtitle: Persistence & Defense Evasion (T1205.002 - Socket Filters)
stages.description: Refusing to open a visible service window that guards check every hour, the spy clips a tiny 30-step mechanical sieve directly onto the main incoming mail chute. Every letter streaming into the building passes silently over that sieve, which ignores ordinary mail and waits only for the spy secret emblem. BPFDoor called socket(AF_PACKET, SOCK_RAW, htons(ETH_P_IP)) to create a raw packet socket and invoked setsockopt(sock, SOL_SOCKET, SO_ATTACH_FILTER, &bpf_prog...) (attaching a 30-instruction classic Berkeley Packet Filter bytecode program into the Linux kernel that inspects every frame arriving on the network card before iptables or nftables firewall rules are evaluated, dropping normal traffic so BPFDoor consumes 0% CPU until a packet containing magic bytes 0x7255 at UDP/ICMP offset or 0x5293 at TCP offset arrives). Because AF_PACKET sockets do not bind a TCP or UDP port, netstat -tlpn, ss -tlpn, and external port scanners (nmap) show zero open backdoor ports, and the attacker can send the magic packet to any port (even ports blocked by iptables or already used by Apache/SSH on port 443/22). Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: Attaching Kernel Berkeley Packet Filter via setsockopt(SO_ATTACH_FILTER) / ⇠#2 ALERT T1205.002) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Linux Host eth0 (Before iptables)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Masqueraded Shell (/dev/shm/kdmtmpflush)).

keySpecs.value: setsockopt(sock, SOL_SOCKET, SO_ATTACH_FILTER, &bpf_prog, sizeof(bpf_prog)) (Checks magic bytes 0x7255 UDP/ICMP or 0x5293 TCP)

Audit active raw packet sockets across Linux servers via `ss -0pb` (which dumps attached BPF bytecode filters) and alert on processes holding `CAP_NET_RAW` that are not legitimate `tcpdump`/`dhclient` binaries.

stages.title: Stage 3: Magic Packet Activation, iptables Port Redirection & Memory-Only PTY Shell
stages.subtitle: Command and Control (T1205.001 - Traffic Signaling)
stages.description: The instant a passing letter carries the secret wax stamp and matching passphrase, the spy wakes up, briefly swings a hidden wall panel to steer the caller around the lobby metal detector, and opens a private, trace-free speaking tube straight into the post office basement. Upon receiving a TCP, UDP, or ICMP Echo packet containing 0x7255 / 0x5293 and a valid password hash, BPFDoor forked a child process, allocated a pseudo-terminal (/dev/ptmx without recording a login in /var/log/wtmp or utmp), and either connected back to the attacker with an RC4-encrypted reverse shell or executed /sbin/iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp -s <attacker_ip> --dport 22 -j REDIRECT --to-ports <ephemeral_port> (hijacking inbound connections on legitimate port 22/80/443 exclusively for the attacker’s source IP while all other users still reached the real SSH/web server). As soon as the interactive session ended, BPFDoor executed iptables -t nat -D PREROUTING ... to delete the temporary NAT redirection rule and return to passive dormancy. In the documented EventID 1 exchange from Linux Host eth0 (Before iptables) to Raw Socket BPF Filter (0x7255 / 0x5293), Raw Socket BPF Filter (0x7255 / 0x5293) responds with ALERT 1 (confirming that the /sbin/iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp -s 198.51.100.204 --dport 22 -j REDIRECT --to-ports 42391 request succeeded on Raw Socket BPF Filter (0x7255 / 0x5293) and completing the final execution objective of BPFDoor Passive Linux Rootkit & Classic BPF Magic Packet Filter (Red Menshen)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ /sbin/iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp -s 198.51.100.204 --dport 22 -j REDIRECT --to-ports 42391 / ⇠#3 ALERT 1) from Node ③ (#3 Linux Host eth0 (Before iptables)) to Node ④ (#4 Raw Socket BPF Filter (0x7255 / 0x5293)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Masqueraded Shell (/dev/shm/kdmtmpflush)).
